discipline_framing: Qualitative digital ethnography and consumer research applied to online community behavior and the digital tribes of Gen Z and Gen Alpha
audience: Trend analysts, consumer researchers, brand strategists, UX researchers, and academics who must understand online communities from the inside — meanings, norms, and behaviors that metrics alone cannot reveal
sources: Kozinets, Netnography: The Essential Guide to Qualitative Social Media Research (and its successive editions) — the founding method
Hine, Virtual Ethnography and Ethnography for the Internet — internet ethnography foundations
Geertz's thick description and classical ethnographic fieldwork tradition (immersion, participant observation)
boyd, It's Complicated — networked teens' social lives, and Ito et al., Hanging Out, Messing Around, and Geeking Out
Arnould & Thompson's consumer culture theory (CCT) program connecting ethnography to markets
Charmaz, Constructing Grounded Theory, and Braun & Clarke's thematic analysis for qualitative coding
Association of Internet Researchers (AoIR) ethical guidelines for internet research
pitfalls: Treating public visibility as ethical clearance — public data can still harm vulnerable communities when analyzed and reported
Drive-by research: scraping posts without immersion, missing the norms, in-jokes, and context that make data interpretable
Assuming online personas equal offline identities, or that vocal community members represent the silent majority
Extracting subcultural insights for commercial use without credit, consent, or community benefit
Letting the analyst's own platform fluency (or illiteracy) bias interpretation — reflexivity omitted
